Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, I hereby declare open the 11th meeting of the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council. And we will begin the high-level panel discussion on the 15th anniversary of the United Nations Declaration on Human Rights Education and Training, good practices, challenges, and the way forward, held pursuant to Council Resolution 57/10. That panel discussion will focus on human rights education for, with, and by children and youth, perspectives and practices. This debate is accessible to persons with disabilities through the provision of international sign interpretation and real-time captioning, together with the other accessibility means. I encourage those who may need reasonable accommodation to inform the Secretariat if they haven't done so already. It is my honor to welcome to the podium Mr. Volker Turk, United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, who will deliver an opening statement. It is also my honor to welcome our distinguished panelists. Her Excellency Ms. Davaasuren Gerelmaa, Permanent Representative from Mongolia to the United Nations Office and other international organizations in Geneva. Mr. Goran Georgiev, Regional Director at the World Organization of the Scout Movement. Ms. Marion Wanyuku Mutugi, Commissioner of the Kenyan National Commission on Human Rights. And Mr. Alessandro Ienzi, Artistic Director at the Rasis Teatro, Be Human, Be Yourself. Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, the list of speakers will close in 15 minutes. I encourage all speakers to intervene in an interactive way, present comments and ask questions that reflect the panelists' interventions and the discussion. The speaking time limit is one minute and 30 seconds for all, and a maximum of 40 speakers will be accommodated. Delegates inscribed on the list of speakers who cannot take the floor because of time constraints can upload their statements to the online system to be posted on the HRC portal. And without further ado, I now give the floor to Mr. High Commissioner Volker Türk. You have the floor.

Thank you very much, Madam Vice President, Excellencies, distinguished participants. In 1980, smallpox became the first and so far the only human disease to be eradicated through prevention in the absence of treatment. Over the past century, the death rate from natural disasters fell by more than 90 percent even as those disasters became more common, again, because we became better prepared. Time and again, humanity has turned to prevention as the most effective and efficient response to deadly diseases, to natural hazards, or economic shocks. Sometimes it's the only response available. When it comes to conflict, crisis, and injustice, Prevention is far better than the cure. And we have an effective vaccine against many of society's ills, human rights education. Human rights education strengthens our collective immunity against hatred, violence, discrimination, and polarization of all kinds. By teaching us our rights, enabling critical thinking, fostering solidarity and compassion, and awakening our conscience, it helps stop these malignancies at their source before they take hold and spread. And governments know this well. That is why 15 years ago, the United Nations adopted the Declaration on Human Rights Education and Training. And the declaration affirmed that all states have a responsibility to provide education about, through, and for human rights to everyone. The authors of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights knew this too. By embedding human rights education in the text, they equipped the declaration with an engine through which each generation can renew its power. And by the way, human rights education was also embedded in the statute that created my office. For society as a whole, human rights education helps us resist dehumanization, break cycles of tension and violence, and live side by side in harmony with each other and the planet. For governments, it helps build trust, reinforce social cohesion, strengthen security, and foster resilience. For children and young people, human rights education gives them the tools to stand up for themselves and their peers in the real world and online. For the quiet majority, understanding human rights offers clarity, hope, and a compass for navigating the extremes of our divided world. And for all of us working for human rights, it helps us step beyond our own bubble and connect with people in ways that resonate deeply. Madam Vice President, the vaccine I'm talking about has already been tested many times and in many places, and it works. In Colombia, education based on art and storytelling has become a powerful tool for peacebuilding, helping young people, including former child soldiers, build empathy and trust. In Northern Ireland, integrated schools have brought together students from different religious communities, helping to challenge prejudice and bridge historic divides. Human rights education has also proved to be invaluable in humanitarian settings. In Jordan, for example, it has promoted the inclusion and participation of Syrian refugee children. So the evidence is clear, human rights education is not a nice to have, but a necessity for every society. So why don't we invest in it fully, consistently and seriously? I welcome the efforts of 34 states that have reported on their progress in human rights education, but this is clearly not enough. Human rights education is still not mandatory across all countries and the education systems. Major gaps remain in legislation, policies, curricula, and teacher training. It troubles me deeply when I hear of economists, of security services, of people working in digital technology, and even government ministers who have little or no understanding of human rights or what they mean for their work. Where does this leave us when addressing complex challenges like the climate crisis, technological developments, which we all see are both increasingly slipping beyond our control? The entire digital tech sector needs a crash course on human rights immediately. Madam Vice-President, today I am calling on every state to make human rights education compulsory at all levels, primary, secondary, tertiary, and in all disciplines, not just when it comes to law or social science. With less than 20% of countries reporting progress, the world is still far from a passing grade. We need to aim for excellence. I ask all states to report back by the 80th anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 2028. People of all professions everywhere should know their rights and understand how their choices and their decisions affect the rights of others. Both formal and extracurricular programs, including children and youth movements, arts and sport, can help us get there. Very happy that we have the panelists here representing some of these areas. The freedom, dignity, and equal worth of every person need to be the golden thread running through all subjects and materials from textbooks and maps to digital tools. Programs for children and young people need to be built with and by them and reflect their lived realities. My office is ready to work with governments, with civil society, with educators, with children and youth movements to bring such learning to everyone. From Mongolia to South Africa, we are supporting laws, policies and practices that promote inclusive education grounded in human rights. And our new Global Alliance for Human Rights will be a laboratory for solutions, not only to repel mounting assaults on people's rights, but to preempt them. That is why Rights in Every Classroom is one of the Alliance's first flagship initiatives. It will pull ideas and resources from everywhere to make human rights education standard in schools and universities worldwide, and it will help reach the goal we need to achieve by 2028. The strongest defense of human rights lies with people who understand them, who claim them, and stand up for them. This is our best way to push back against defeatism, hopelessness, alienation, and apathy. I look forward to working with all of you to make this a reality and to take stock of our collective progress in two years to come. Thank you very much.

I thank you for your opening remarks and clear call on all states. I will now give the floor to the distinguished panelists for their initial presentations. And first, I give the floor to Her Excellency, Mrs. Dawasuuren Gerelmaa. Please, you have the floor.

Madam Vice President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, Mongolia has long recognized that human rights education is an important foundation for building a culture of human rights. Our experience predated the adoption of the United Nations Declaration on Human Rights Education and Training and has evolved over time in line with its principles. As early as 1997, Mongolia introduced a dedicated human rights course into higher education institution, providing legal training, making an early step toward institutionalizing human rights education within the national education system. We subsequently took steps to extend human rights education into secondary education, including through measures under the 2011 to 2014 action plan, responding to the recommendations received through the universal periodic review. This commitment has been further strengthened through the subsequent action plan for 2016 to 2019 and most recently for 2026 to 2030. We worked closely with the National Human Rights Commission, international partners such as UNDP and OHCHR, and a wide range of other stakeholders to implement the awareness raising and training activities identified in those action plans. Today, we are taking a further step by strengthening the legal and institutional foundation for human rights education across the entire education system. In 2023, Mongolia adopted a revised general law on education, which provides a legal basis for the mandatory inclusion of human rights education in curricula at all levels of education. This is an important step because it moves human rights education from being an optional activity towards becoming an integral component of the education system, from pre-primary and primary education through secondary, vocational and technical education to higher education, with content adopted to the age and learning needs of students. Madam Vice President, Mongolia adopted its first national human rights program in 2003 and work is now well advanced on a second national human rights program envisaged as a long-term 10-year framework for strengthening the protection and promotion of the human rights. The intention is for the new program to be more than a statement of principles. It's envisioned in an implementable, people-centered development framework that can guide successive governments over the common decade. This is in particular relevant to the human rights education. The renewal of the National Human Rights Program provides an opportunity to connect education, institutional capacity and implementation much more systematically. We have also sought to ensure the curricula reform is informed by broad national dialogue. In 2025, the Ministry of Education together with the National Human Rights Commission, Amnesty International Mongolia and the United Nations Resident Coordinators Office convened the Human Rights Education Symposium, the fourth of its series since 2017, in the context of the fifth phase of the World Programme for Human Rights Education. More than 100 researchers and experts from government, from national human rights commissions, civil society, and international organizations participated. One important outcome was the development of a matrix identifying the human rights education content to be incorporated across all levels of education. This matrix is now informing the revision of curricula and education materials. Madam Vice President, looking ahead, Mongolia is seeking to contribute not only nationally but also regionally. In its Human Rights 75th pledge, Mongolia committed to establish a human rights regional human rights training and research center in Ulaanbaatar. In fact, it is a hub for education, research, and capacity building for governments. national human rights institutions, civil society and academia across the region. During the visit of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Mr. Walter Turk, to Mongolia in May this year, Mongolia and OHCHR signed a roadmap towards the establishment of this center. This marks an important milestone in translating our commitment into concrete action. We recognize that significant work now lies ahead to make this vision a reality, and we look forward to working closely with OHCHR and partners across the region. Distinguished colleagues, Mongolia's experience demonstrated that human rights education can be strengthened when it is supported substantially by legislation, national policy, curriculum reform, teacher preparation, institutional cooperation, and sustained national dialogue. We recognize that implementation is an ongoing process. We see human rights education not simply as a subject to be taught, But there's a culture to be cultivated, is a culture grounded in equality, dignity, participation, respect, and peaceful resolution of differences. As we look toward the future, we believe that our collective focus should increasingly be on moving from commitments to institutionalization, implementation, and measurable impact. Mongolia stands ready to continue sharing its experience, learn from others, and work with all partners to ensure that human rights education becomes a lasting investment in human dignity, democracy, and peaceful inclusive society. I thank you, Madam Vice President.
Thank you very much for outlining examples and experiences of Mongolia. Next, I give the floor to Mr. Goran Georgiev. Please, you have the floor.

Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates and colleagues, it is an honor to be participating in this high-level panel marking the 15th anniversary of the United Nations Declaration on Human Rights Education and Training. As Regional Director of the World Organization of the Scout Movement, I bring perspective of global education movement that engage millions of young people across the world in non-formal education. The anniversary that we celebrate today is an important opportunity to reflect not only on the progress, but also to recognize an important reality. Human rights education is most effective when it moves beyond awareness and becomes practice. Young people do not become defenders of human rights simply by learning about the rights. They become defenders of human rights by practicing respect, participation, inclusion, solidarity, and responsibility in their everyday lives. This is where Scouting contributes. Learning about human rights for human rights and through human rights, as High Commissioner mentioned. Worldwide, Scouting delivers human rights education through experimental learning. Young people learn by doing. Through teamwork, democratic decision-making, community service, intercultural dialogue, peacebuilding, and leadership opportunities, they develop values and practice participation rather than learning only about it. They exercise responsibility towards others rather than treating it as an abstract. In other words, human rights becomes part of their everyday life. Our collaboration with the United Nations has strengthened this work significantly. Through partnership across the UN system, including with the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, the World Health Organization, and UNICEF, Scouting has been able to connect global human rights standards with practical projects at local level. In recent years, we have strengthened our collaboration with the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, and through initiatives such as the Power of Human Rights Education, young leaders from more than 16 countries have been able to strengthen their competencies in human rights education and active citizenship through non-formal learning. This cooperation has continued through the WUSM co-chair role in the UN NGO Working Group on Human Rights Education and Learning, contributing to shaping the fifth phase of the World Programme and the pioneering educational initiatives co-developed with our World Scout Centre. A dedicated human rights education program forms part of the center's permanent education offer and reach thousands of young people from around the world every year. Every day, Scouts lead community projects promoting social inclusion, supporting displaced populations, advancing gender equality, protect nature, and responding to the humanitarian needs. Our experience highlights three important lessons. First, Non-formal education is essential to assure the full realization of the formal education. Schools provide essential formal education opportunities and non-formal provides ability to develop competencies, life skills and internalize values. In many countries, Scoutit works closely with the Ministry of Education on creating partnerships, with work in environments where human rights are not only taught in the classrooms, but also lived through participation, leadership and service. Second, human rights are the best learned through experience. When young people participate in decisions, engage in dialogue across differences, resolve conflicts peacefully, serve their communities and work alongside people from diverse backgrounds. Human rights then moved from theory in practice. Human rights discussions often focus on the distinction between right holders and duty barriers. In World Scouting, young people are active participants, beneficiaries, and advocates for themselves and for others. They are recognized as partners and leaders. Through the U-Act initiatives, Responding to the consequences of the war in Ukraine, tens of thousands of Scouts provided humanitarian assistance, created safe spaces, supported displaced families, and provided non-formal education, fostering inclusion and solidarity. Young people were not simply receiving support; they were helping to defend dignity and uphold the rights of others. Inclusion must be intentional and proactive. If human rights education is to fulfill its promise, it must reach all children and young people, including those who face barriers because of disability, displacement, poverty, geography, or other forms of marginalization. This requires partnerships among governments, civil society organizations, schools, communities, national human rights institutions, and youth-led movements. no single actor can achieve this alone. Through initiatives such as the Ticket to Life, Scouting supports refugees, displaced children, and other young people facing difficult circumstances. By participating in Scouting, they gain confidence, skills, belonging, and opportunities to contribute to their communities. Looking ahead, The fifth phase of the World Programme for Human Rights Education, with its focus on children and youth and its emphasis on digital technologies and gender equality, offers an important opportunity. We should invest not only on the curriculum development and educational resources, but also in youth participation, community-based learning and the strengthening of the non-formal education spaces. The world today faces growing polarization, misinformation, conflict and social fragmentation. Human rights education is therefore not a luxury. It's an investment for social cohesion, democratic participation and peaceful society. As we mark 15 years of the declaration, let us reaffirm a simple but powerful commitment. Every child and every young people should have the opportunity not only to know their rights, but also to exercise them, uphold them, and stand up for the rights of others. Thank you.

Thank you very much for your perspectives and giving us also the insights on the role of the youth organizations. Next, I have the honour to give the floor to Ms. Marion Wainiku Mutungi. Please, you have the floor.

Madam Vice President, Excellencies, Ambassadors, distinguished panelists and colleagues, the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights is honored to participate in this high-level panel discussion on the 15th anniversary of the United Nations Declaration on Human Rights Education and Training. I want to focus my remarks on a practical question that every national human rights institution faces. Once a state commits to human rights education, how do we know that this commitment reaches the classroom? In Kenya, we sought to answer this using SDG 4.7, human rights education monitoring tool. This is a web-based tool developed by the Danish Institute for Human Rights with its indicators developed in consultation with the Office of the High Commission for Human Rights. It translates SDG indicator 4.7.1 into a structured evidence-based self-assessment measuring distinct elements. One, national education policies. Two, curricula. Three, teacher education. Four, student assessment. And last but not least, the learning environment. At the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights, established under Article 57 of our constitution, this NHRI is accredited as an A status under the Paris Principles, and we partnered with the Ministry of Education in February 2021 to pilot this survey. We targeted three counties chosen to reflect Kenya's urban, peri-urban, and rural realities through the counties of Nairobi, Machakos, and Kajiado. Through focus group discussions, key informant interviews, and questionnaires, we reached 230 respondents who included policymakers, county directors of education, teachers, and students themselves. Madam Vice President, we are pleased to note that Kenya's overall score was 67%. Although this represents meaningful progress, the desegregated data revealed gaps that matter far more than the headline number. We found human rights content genuinely present across the curriculum in subjects like social studies, history, government, religious education, and English. Overall, 85% of respondents confirmed that textbooks feature explicit illustrations and pictures reflecting the human rights principles. But there are three gaps that stood out. Number one, policy participation. 78% of the respondents said that National policies were developed with little or no participation from county and sub-county actors. The very people responsible for implementing them were left out. Two, resource allocation. 60% of the policy makers identified limited financial allocation from the national budget to operationalize human rights education. Three, the learning environment. 84% of the schools we visited had no trained professional counselors and 61% lacked infrastructure accessible to learners with disabilities, such as ramps, adapted sanitation facilities, and the very basics that they require to learn. Madam Vice President, we did not stop at measurement. Consistent with our constitutional mandate to secure observance of democratic values and human rights standards by state organs, the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights issued a formal advisory to the Ministry of Education in August 2021. This recommended a bottom-up approach to policy formulation, dedicated budgetary allocation, and human rights division within the Ministry, as well as functioning complaint mechanisms in every school. We approach this as more than a compliance exercise. Education in Kenya is not only a developmental strategy under our vision 2030, it is a fundamental right in itself consistent with the human rights principle of interdependence. The right to education, we recognise, has a ripple effect on the realisation of every other right. On this basis, the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights also proposed a framework of cooperation with the Ministry of Education to mainstream human rights indicators into curriculum development and jointly monitor progress against national and international obligations. I am pleased to report that within the five years since administration of this tool, this cooperation has materialized into a formal, memorandum of understanding between the Kenya National Commission of Human Rights and Kenya Institute of Curriculum Development, the KICD. In addition, there's a memorandum of understanding between KNCHR and various universities across the counties. This is to build capacity as well as explicitly embed human rights education into curriculum. Madam Vice President, we are conscious that surveying three of Kenya's 47 counties only gave us a baseline and not a complete national audit. But that baseline is a fixed point we can now return to as Kenya's competence-based curriculum continues to roll out. And it gave us, our national conversation on human rights education, something it lacked. a shared evidence-based starting point against which government, civil society, and the commission can hold one another accountable. Five years later, we propose that we could measure the progress or lack thereof as Kenya rolls out this competency-based curriculum, and this time to a more representative sample. I thank you.

Thank you very much for sharing insights of the work and the role of national human rights institutions. And last but certainly not least, I have the honour to give the floor to Mr. Alessandro Ienzi. Please, you have the floor.

Excellencies, distinguished representatives, colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, good morning and thank you for the opportunity to be here today. My name is Alessandro Ienzi. I'm a theater director and artist. I'm a human rights lawyer and founder and artistic director of Raices Teatro, which is a nonprofit organization based in Palermo, Sicily, Italy, which is now active all over the world and promoting human rights education through the heart and theater. I would like to begin with a simple idea that has guided my work and is now guiding the work of the NGO and of the theater company. Human rights are not only principles that we must teach, they are experiences that people must be able to live, like the right to speak, the right to be heard, the right to participate, and the right to imagine a future if we talk about young people. These are not just words, these are experiences that we must allow people to live. Throughout my work, I've asked myself just one question. What happened when a person, and specifically when a young person, loses the possibility of imagining a future? I've asked this in schools, in communities across Sicily, while working especially with unaccompanied migrant children, with young people in Egypt, in Nepal, in Senegal, in Palestine, in Northeast Nigeria, and in many contexts marked by violence and conflict. The contexts are different, this is true, but one thing remains the same. Before a young person can participate in society, they must believe that their voice has a value. And this is where human rights education meets artistic practice. At Raizis, for this reason, we use theatre, creative writing, movement, football freestyle, visual arts and collective creation to create spaces where young people can transform experience into dialogue and dialogue into participation. But we don't give people a voice because people already have a voice. Our responsibility is to create the conditions for that voice to be heard. And Sicily, this approach has been developed especially through the Lab School, which is an educational model created by SHE Sicily, which is Schools for Health in Europe, which is a network of nine schools from nine cities, in cooperation with the Sicilian region department for education and vocational training, and in cooperation with RAICES. And the program connects artistic practice, human rights education, and youth participation. Together, we address issues such as addiction, violence, social exclusion, emotional vulnerability, identity and peer pressure. Our experience is clear. Prevention cannot rely just only on information and/or fear, but it must also be based on participation, trust, relationships and creativity. Through our theater activity in Sicily, we have engaged approximately 30,000 young people per year, and we are currently training 27 young people through an intensive performing art workshop, which is called Officina delle Arti, now hosted by the Istituto Florio in Erice, near Trapani, and managed by Istituto Rizzo in Melilli. And this school is including dance, theater, creative writing, and football freestyle. In particular, this section is managed by Mr. William Koschak, which will be performing today on childhood, which is our performing now, touring all over the world. 00 p.m., so feel free also to attend the side event at Auditorium 200H. The program also got the contribution of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, responsible for human rights education and training, and this strengthened the connection between artistic practice and international human rights education. So for us, what's clear through the presentation of our theater show, but also through the creation of our theater show with young people, is that human rights education cannot remain theoretical. It must become an experience. And this is particularly important, for example, when working with unaccompanied migrant children. Sicily is often a place of arrival. Many young people are arriving from African countries, crossing the desert, crossing the sea. But arrival is not just the end of a journey, because it is a beginning of a new challenge. belonging, identity, language, education, and finding a place in a new society. These are important challenges. And through artistic creation, we create spaces where young people can express themselves and participate. Because behind every migration statistic, every procedure, every number, every policy, there is always a person, a young person with memories, with fears, with dreams, with talents, and with a future. Our objective is not to speak on behalf of young people, it is to create the condition for them to speak for themselves. The same principle guided our work in Egypt through Together with Rai, developed in cooperation with IOM Egypt, where young people from different backgrounds from Egypt, but also from Sudan and Gaza, use theater and artistic practices as tools for expression, inclusion, and for leadership. So our question is not what can we do for them, but what can we create together? And this difference is very important because people cannot be defined only through their vulnerability. They must be recognized for what they can create, what they can contribute, and what can become. I've seen the same principle in northeastern Nigeria in cooperation with UNODC in contexts marked by violence and instability. because art cannot erase trauma, but it can create spaces where young people are not reduced to their trauma. Spaces where they can rediscover imagination, express themselves, share their stories, and imagine possibilities beyond violence. Today, this vision continues with our project, Roots of the Mediterranean, which is now touring all over the Mediterranean. The Mediterranean is often described through borders, migration, conflicts, also through division, but it is also a space of our shared memory, cultural exchange and encounter. Through the programme we work with young people, artists and communities across different countries. We listen, Before we can speak, we meet, and then we represent. We create before we judge. Because human rights education must also become an education in encounter. My experience from Sicily to Egypt, from Nigeria to Nepal, from Senegal to Palestine, has taught me something very simple. Young people do not simply need us to talk about their future. They need to participate in building it. For this reason, I believe that artistic and cultural practices should have more central role in human rights education. Every human being carries a story, and every story has the potential to create a connection. Thank you.

Thank you for sharing with us examples and practices from NGO perspective. Excellencies, dear participants, we will now proceed with the first segment of the list of speakers. All interventions from the floor are limited to one minute and 30 seconds. The list of speakers is now closed. And first, I have the honor to give the floor to European Union.

Thank you, Madam Vice Chair. I have the honor to speak on behalf of the European Union. We thank the High Commissioner for his compelling keynote and the panelists for sharing their insights and good practices. 15 years after its adoption, the United Nations Declaration on Human Rights Education and Training remains a vital framework for bringing universal rights into everyday life. We welcome progress in translating its commitment into concrete actions in classrooms, communities, and beyond. Human rights education enables people to understand and exercise their rights, respect those of others, and participate meaningfully in society. Building on this progress requires continued political will, sustained investment in education, inclusive learning, and strong partnerships. The EU fully supports the World Programme for Human Rights Education, including its ongoing fifth phase and focused on children and youth. By addressing some of today's most pressing challenges, it connects human rights education to their everyday lives, making their voices and experiences essential to its effective implementation. The EU also welcomes the synergies between the declaration, the world program, and the Global Alliance for Human Rights, Rights in Every Classroom initiatives. Dear panelists, what further concrete steps can States take through their policies and partnerships to strengthen human rights education and broaden its reach, including through the Global Alliance? I thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Venezuela on behalf of a group of countries.

Thank you, Madam Vice-President. We make this statement on behalf of the Group of Friends in Defence of the United Nations Charter On this 15th anniversary of the United Nations Declaration on Human Rights Education and Training, our group reaffirms the importance of education for the promotion and implementation of all human rights. Education is a fundamental human right and an essential tool for the promotion of peace, justice, solidarity, sustainable development and human rights. We reaffirm our commitment to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, including SDG 4, to ensure free, quality education. It is necessary to address the increase in structural inequality, polarization, lack of opportunities, and to demand fulfillment of financing commitments for development. We express concern that over 770 million young people and adults are illiterate and over 250 million children, adolescents, and young people are out of school. Our group calls for the mobilization of international financial resources and technical cooperation, as well as capacity building, to bring lifelong learning opportunities to people. These are based on contributions rather than penalizing. The right to education must be implemented for all. Thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Democratic Republic of the Congo on behalf of, uh, Group des Etats Membres de la Francophonie.

Madame Vice-President, I make this group on behalf of the group of Francophone ambassadors who welcome this panel because education commits to human rights, democracy and is at the heart of our commitments. We welcome the adoption by the Chair of the resolution on education for peace and reaffirm the role of education in promoting peace, tolerance and respect for human rights. Given the rise in hate speech, discrimination and attacks on freedom, we must strengthen human rights in education systems. We welcome the initiatives of the Global Alliance for Human Rights in the Classroom, which seek to bring human rights into primary and secondary education. We also welcome the adoption in 2023 by UNESCO of the recommendation on education for peace, human rights and sustainable development, on which a flagship programme is being developed. We emphasise the importance of empowering young people and ensuring that we have safe, inclusive educational environments. We reaffirm the importance of resources in French and in local languages to ensure that linguistic minorities and all others may be included in the process. How can multi-stakeholders partnerships improve access to multilingual resources and ensure human rights education for all?
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Slovenia on behalf of a group of countries.

Thank you, Madam Vice President. I have the honor to speak on behalf of the platform of member states on human rights education and training, comprising Brazil, Costa Rica, Italy, Morocco, the Philippines, Senegal, Thailand, and my own country, Slovenia. Our countries have long championed this agenda, including through the World Program for Human Rights Education, and led the initiative for today's panel. We thank the High Commissioner and panelists for their valuable contributions. Fifteen years after its adoption, the United Nations Declaration on Human Rights Education and Training remains a shared foundation for advancing a universal culture of human rights. Human rights education brings this vision to life, equipping people to understand and exercise their rights, respect those of others, and participate meaningfully in society. We are encouraged by active engagement with the Declaration and the World Programme, and by progress in translating their objectives into concrete action around the world. The World Programme's fifth phase, focusing on children and youth, offers an opportunity to build on these achievements. Ahead of its mid-term review, we encourage all stakeholders to share good practices, identify gaps, and strengthen implementation. Today's discussion offers valuable lessons for taking the work forward, and we hope this anniversary inspires renewed commitment and sustained action. I thank you.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Nigeria on behalf of a group of countries.

Thank you, Madam Vice President. I have the honor to deliver the statement on behalf of the Group of Friends of the Family. We take note with appreciation of the convening of this panel, marking the 15th anniversary of the UN Declaration on Human Rights Education and Training. The family, as a natural and fundamental group unit of society entitled to protection by society and the state, is the first environment in which children learn about dignity, equality, and respect for others. Through daily interaction and parental guidance, these principles become part of how children understand their own rights and treat others around them. For human rights education to take root, lessons taught in the classroom need to find expression in everyday life. A strong partnership between the family and schools can help children learn to listen, resolve disagreements peacefully, reject discrimination, and show solidarity with others. Through this partnership, children experience human rights as values practiced at home, at school, and in relationship with others. This requires equipping parents with practical educational resources and respecting their responsibilities, rights, and duties to provide appropriate direction and guidance, consistent with children's evolving capacities and best interests. Supporting the family's educational role is therefore an investment in the culture of human rights that each generation can carry forward. Finally, we ask the panelists, how can national human rights education programs better support the family in fulfilling this role? I thank you, Madam Vice President.
Thank you. Next, I give the floor to Benin on behalf of a group of countries.

Thank you, Madam Vice-President. I have the honour to take the floor on behalf of the beneficiaries for the LDC process. We thank the Office of the High Commissioner and the panellists for this debate, which comes at a time when human rights education must fully be part of climate imperatives. For small island developing states and for many coastal countries, the climate emergency is already threatening the rights to life, water, food and decent housing. Human rights education and training must therefore become tools for empowerment civic action and resilience in the face of environmental disasters, beyond the mere theoretical teaching of fundamental freedoms. International solidarity must go beyond post-disaster relief To invest in prevention and human capacities, we call for a strengthening of skills transfer, for interregional sharing of educational innovations, and for sustainable funding for climate-smart human rights education programmes. Investing in human rights education in the context of the climate challenge means preparing the conscience of future generations to guarantee the dignity, justice and continuity of our peoples. Thank you.

This requires oversight and monitoring, particularly in the field of technology. With regard to the question on due diligence benchmarks, the working group considers that effective due diligence must extend beyond traditional compliance mechanisms. States should require technology providers, companies, private actors operating in security contexts to identify beneficial ownership structures, conduct human rights impact assessments before deploying high-risk technologies, and maintain records of subcontracting relationships, establish traceability mechanisms. Importantly, commercial confidentiality should not be a shield against accountability. Finally, in terms of the third dimension, support the open-ended intergovernmental working group on PMSEs and the adoption of the international regulatory instrument to cover the activities of PMSEs. The working group notes the broad interest expressed in this room yesterday regarding strengthening norms around private military security actors and the use of emerging technologies. This brings me to the last questions on recruitment and cross-border activities. Again, to close gaps, states should sign and commit to the conventions in place. As we heard in the room yesterday, many states are grappling with predatory recruitment, particularly the transnational and technological dimensions of recruitment that relies on deceptive promises. It is clear that the global mercenary market is surging, rooted in the proliferation of armed conflicts across the world today, sustained by states who organize, recruit, supply, finance, arm, and equip mercenaries, contractors, and predatory recruits to sustain conflicts over resources, territory, and strategic influences. Mercenarism is therefore more than the individual. The global mercenary market is tied to states of origin, states of transit, and states of destination, And this creates perverse incentives for participation, profitable informal and formal economies, and reinforces the neocolonial dynamics of global warfare and labor, whereby subcontracting violence to and labor from the global south. State cooperation is required here. States need to respect calls from states in the Global South for their nationals not to be recruited into foreign wars, for their nationals not to be used as disposable soldiers, and for their domestic laws which ban serving in foreign armed conflicts and foreign armed forces to be respected. Allow me to conclude. Technology itself is not the problem. These can contribute to peace and security. The challenge lies in preventing the misuse by actors operating with insufficient oversight and outside accountability frameworks. No state can address these challenges alone. The working group stands ready with states to offer technical cooperation and assistance, and for NGOs and CSOs, we welcome consultations and submissions with a clarification that we are not an investigative body. I thank you, Madam Vice-President.

Mrs. Vice President, Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, Dear Families of Victims, Representatives of Civil Society, and National Human Rights Institutions, It is a great honor to address the Human Rights Council in my capacity as Chair-Rapporteur of the Working Group on Enforced and Involuntary Disappearances. I would like to begin by reaffirming our solidarity with all victims of enforced disappearance, including the families of the disappeared. Across the world, relatives and their allies continue to search for disappeared persons. Many do so despite intimidation, harassment, criminalization, and reprisals. Their courage is a constant reminder that enforced disappearance is not confined to the moment when a person is taken. Its consequences continue for as long as the truth remains concealed and families are denied answers and justice. President, During the reporting period, the Working Group transmitted 1,723 new cases of enforced disappearance to 36 States. This is the highest number recorded by the Working Group in an annual reporting period over the past decade, reflecting the growing demand on its humanitarian mandate. Yet, these figures do not reflect the full scale of enforced disappearance. Our records are only the tip of the iceberg, as many cases are not brought to our attention due, among other factors, to lack of access or fear of reprisal. During the reporting period, the Working Group clarified 374 cases. While every clarification means that the Working Group was able to establish the fate and whereabouts of the disappeared person, it does not necessarily mean that the person has returned to their loved ones. nearly 60% of all clarification have been made only after the disappeared person's death was established. This sobering reality reminds us that time is most often the most critical factor in cases of enforced disappearances. Excellencies, 46 years after the establishment of the working group, enforced disappearance remains a global phenomenon, but the context in which it occurs have changed considerably. In 1980, the Working Group dealt primarily with disappearances associated with military dictatorships. Today, the actors, methods, and justification may change, but the purpose remains the same, to place a person outside the protection of the law, conceal the truth, and create a chilling effect. The Working Group remains particularly concerned by the continued use of enforced disappearances in armed conflict, including against civilians and, in particular, children. This is notable in the context of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, as well as in Gaza and in Sudan. The Working Group is also concerned by unlawful cross-border transfers, transnational repressions, deportation and returns that expose individuals to a risk of enforced disappearances, including in Tanzania, Kenya, the United States of America and Thailand. The Working Group is further concerned by the use of national security and counter-terrorism frameworks to conceal the fate and whereabouts of detained persons, particularly in Egypt, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. Finally, it is concerned by the use of enforced disappearances in the context of the suspension of democratic guarantees, including in El Salvador and Nicaragua. Excellencies, during the reporting period, the Working Group also undertook a study on enforced disappearances and memorialization. The study highlights memorialization as a crucial form of operation for enforced disappearances and as an integral component of the right to truth. Memorialization must be grounded in international human rights law and developed in close cooperation with victims, including families of disappeared persons, as well as civil society. The working group is further presenting its follow up report on the implementation of the recommendations made following its visit to Uruguay in 2022. The working group welcomes Uruguay's cooperation and notes progress in efforts to locate and identify disappeared persons. Challenges remain, including limited access to archives, resources for searches, and a comprehensive reparation framework for victims and their relatives. The working group encourages Uruguay to continue advancing truth, justice, memory, and reparation, and remains available to continue its constructive dialogue with the authorities, victims, and civil society. The reporting period also brought positive developments. The Working Group warmly welcomes Estonia's accession to the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearances. The Working Group would like to thank the Government of Cote d'Ivoire for hosting its annual out-of-Geneva session in May 2026, which allowed to bolster its relationship with relatives organizations, civil society and institutions, as well as of regional and sub-regional human rights mechanisms in Africa. The working group is furthermore thankful for the support received, including through voluntary financial contribution from France, Lithuania and the Republic of Korea. We also reaffirm our thanks to Bangladesh, Canada, Maldives, and the Republic of Korea for the invitations to undertake country visits previously extended to the Working Group. These invitations demonstrate openness to cooperation and constructive engagement with the mandate. Regrettably, despite these invitations, the Working Group was unable to undertake a country visit during the reporting period. The country visit to Guatemala in June 2026, for which we thank the government for agreeing to, will be covered in the next reporting period. The lack of visits in this reporting period was not due to a lack of cooperation from the state concerned or the willingness of the working group. It was a direct consequence of the liquidity crisis affecting the United Nations and the special procedure system. An invitation that cannot be acted upon is a lost opportunity for dialogue, prevention, and technical cooperation. Despite these constraints, the working group provided technical cooperation during the reporting period to Peru, continued cooperation with Bangladesh, Colombia, and Chile, initiated cooperation with the Gambia, and will start cooperation with Guatemala. We remain ready to assist states and institutions seeking to strengthen their responses to enforced disappearance. While the annual number of cases brought before the mandate has risen sharply, its capacity has not increased accordingly. On the contrary, the liquidity crisis has affected its capacity. The Working Group has over 50,000 cases under active consideration. There are now more than 8,000 cases awaiting registration, review, or processing. We are deeply conscious that this backlog is not merely a collection of files. For many families, the Working Group is the only international mechanism to which they can turn in cases of enforced disappearance. When a submission cannot be reviewed promptly, the Working Group may lose the opportunity to intervene during the period when urgent international attention could make the greatest difference. We cannot know how many outcomes might have been different, but we do know that delay has human consequences. The Working Group and its Secretariat continue to handle an unprecedented volume of work with dedication and professionalism, while being asked to do considerably more with less. Adequate capacity is essential to sustain our work. Ms. President, Excellencies, The Working Group calls upon all States: To cooperate fully and promptly with its humanitarian procedure; To investigate every allegation of enforced disappearance independently, impartially, thoroughly and effectively; To protect victims, including relatives, as well as lawyers, human rights defenders and civil society organizations from reprisal and harassment; To respect the prohibition of refoulement. To support truth, justice, reparation and memorialization processes. To ratify or accede to the International Convention and recognize the competences of the Committee on Enforced Disappearances to receive individual or interstate complaints. To honor the pledges made in January 2025 on the occasion of the First World Congress on Enforced Disappearances, as well as to secure a second edition to promote universal ratification and implementation of the Convention. to provide the working group and the special procedure system with the resources necessary to fulfill their mandate effectively. Every enforced disappearance begins with a person being placed outside the protection of the law. It leaves behind a family searching for answers and a society confronted with silence. The working group will continue to stand with families and to work so that no disappeared person is forgotten, silence is broken, and responses are given. But to achieve these aims, the mandate must be given the means to act in time. Thank you very much for your attention.
